name: Java
title: Java (Java 1.4)

presenceList.meta: R2, R3, Ec6, Ec7, D3, L2

type.text: **Interfaces decouple specification from implementation**: A program is written against an interface, and an implementation is supplied at run time
**There are no generics (before Java 5)**: A collection holds `Object`, so every read is a cast the compiler cannot check
**Reflection reads the structure at run time**: `java.lang.reflect` reaches a field or a method by name, outside the type check
**Null is in every reference**: `NullPointerException` is possible wherever a reference is used, and no non-nullable type says otherwise
**There is no sum type**: A closed set of cases is a class hierarchy, and a `switch` over an `int` constant is not checked for exhaustiveness
**A package is not a boundary**: Every public class is reachable on the classpath, and nothing declares what a library exports
**Inheritance is available**: Unchecked class extension couples a subclass to its superclass unless the class is `final`

construction.text: **A field is mutable unless declared `final`**: A setter is the ordinary way to change state
**A factory method states the contract**: A static method returns a cached instance or a subtype
**A complex object needs a builder**: A telescoping constructor couples the call site to the field order
**Collection order is unpinned**: HashMap iterates in a hash-dependent order the specification does not fix, and the ordered map is the opt-in a disciplined team must choose
**One value, many names**: every object is reached through references, an array's buffer is shared by assignment, and no declaration names the alias set — a defensive copy is a discipline, not a type

memory.text: **The JVM collects garbage**: An unreachable object is reclaimed, so a program never frees memory by hand
**There is no manual deallocation**: A dangling pointer cannot occur in managed code
**A collection pause is part of the timing**: The collector's schedule is not the program's
**The default collector stops the world**: A serial collector pauses every thread
**JNI reaches outside the heap**: A native call is unchecked

**The class entered the declared surface**: Java 1.4 made OutOfMemoryError a thrown value (documented) — the memory-exhaustion patch moved the fault into the catchable class, and the JLS/JavaDoc contract names it

error.text: **A checked exception states a recoverable failure**: `throws IOException` puts the failure in the signature
**An unchecked exception bypasses the signature**: A `RuntimeException` can leave any method, so a caller cannot read the failure set from the type
**Try-catch does not compose**: A failure is handled where it is caught, not mapped over
**`finally` closes the resource**: There is no try-with-resources before Java 7

concurrency.text: **A `Thread` is the unit of concurrency**: A task is a `Runnable` handed to a new thread, and a pool is hand-written
**`wait` and `notify` are the primitives**: A monitor and a condition variable are in the language
**`java.util.concurrent` does not exist yet**: A latch, a queue, and an executor are hand-written or bought
**Shared mutable state is the default**: `synchronized`, `volatile`, and manual locks remain, and nothing detects a race
**A task holds a platform thread**: Each task reserves one until it ends, so the number of tasks is bounded by the platform; Java 21's virtual threads remove the cost

platform.text: **The specifications are public**: The Java Language Specification and the JVM Specification are standards any conforming implementation may implement
**Several vendor runtimes run the same class files**: Sun, IBM, BEA, and Hewlett-Packard each shipped a JVM
**Bytecode is portable**: A class file runs on every platform that hosts a JVM

performance.text: **The JIT optimises the hot path**: A method is compiled after it proves hot
**A GC pause is part of the timing**: The collector decides when memory returns
**Startup pays for interpretation**: A cold JVM interprets until the JIT compiles
**The JDK ships a profiler**: `hprof` and a thread dump are in the distribution

ecosystem.text: **Ant builds the classpath**: A build is an XML script, and a dependency is a jar in a directory
**An application server is the deployment target**: J2EE and EJB set the architecture
**The ecosystem carries old APIs**: The enterprise stack keeps 1990s-era interfaces in service beside a current one
**The IDE is mature**: IntelliJ IDEA and Eclipse compile and debug in 2002
The class file carries a published promise across JDK releases [@javaJLS]

**Serialized objects cross on a published promise**: the stream carries the format version and a per-class serial version UID, and the specification states the current protocol is fully backward and forward compatible, read by JDK 1.1.7 and later [@javaSerSpec]

evolution.text: **Backward compatibility is strong**: A class file from an older release still runs
**A feature release was deliberate**: Java 1.4 was one of the multi-year releases, and it added assertions and NIO
**There is no preview mechanism**: An experimental feature is a flag or an incubator module

domain.text: **Excellent for backend and enterprise work**: The standard choice for a large service
**Strong for distributed systems**: Mature frameworks and a mature runtime
**A rich client is Swing, and the web path is an applet**: A browser plugin runs it, and the plugin is a support burden
**Systems programming is out of reach**: A collector and a managed runtime

learning.text: **Widely taught**: Courses, books, and a large body of examples
**The documentation is exhaustive**: Javadoc and the tutorials
**The surface is large**: The language, the standard library, and the enterprise APIs

syntax.text: **A cast accompanies every collection read**: A type is recovered by a cast the compiler cannot check
**A type is spelled out**: The declaration names the type on both sides
**Checked exception syntax is verbose**: A signature carries the failure set

testing.text: **JUnit is the standard test runner**: Mature and ubiquitous
**Excellent debuggers**: Step-through and breakpoints in the IDE and on the command line

security.text: **Memory safe**: The collector prevents a use after free
**Type safe**: A static check runs before the program
**Deserialization is an attack path**: A crafted stream constructs an object graph the program did not choose
**A null check is the caller's**: A reference can be null, and nothing states the guard

feedback.text: **The compiler reports an error in the editor**: An IDE compiles a file as it is saved, so a type error is reported without a build

reproducibility.text: **No contract the toolchain reads**: the JDK compiler consumes the command line, and the dependency contract lives in third-party build tooling the platform does not ship

tradeoffs: **Checked exceptions vs. composition**: Explicit errors do not compose natively, and a `switch` over a hierarchy is not checked for exhaustiveness
**Backward compatibility vs. modern features**: Old codebases lag behind the language, and the 1990s APIs stay in service
**Null as default vs. safety**: Every reference can be null, and nothing in the type marks the check
**A collection holds `Object`**: A read is a cast, so the element type is a convention the compiler cannot check
**Inheritance vs. composition**: A hierarchy is the only way to express a closed set of cases, and the compiler does not check it
verdict: Java 1.4 is the last release before generics, annotations, and enums, and the score is shaped by that absence: a collection holds `Object`, so every read is a cast the compiler cannot check, and a closed set of cases is a hierarchy or an `int` constant that nothing verifies. It does have interfaces, a checked exception channel, a managed heap, and portable bytecode. Main strength: a managed, standardised runtime with a real interface boundary. Main weakness: no generics, no module boundary, and a null in every reference.
verdictExtra: > **Note:** The score reflects Java 1.4 as assessed: no generics, no annotations, no enums, and no module boundary.

energy.text: Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [@joel2025lowresource; @effibenchx2025].

safety.text: A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.

delivery.note: The class-file format and the binary compatibility rules are published by the JVM specification

data_formats.note: Java's serialization specification publishes the stream protocol: the stream carries the magic number and version, every class descriptor carries a serial version UID, the writer can select a protocol version, the current protocol is stated fully backward and forward compatible, and JDK 1.1.7 and later read both protocol versions
